claims.text: The starting composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments within a copper matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites tend to develop phase separation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites tend to develop interfacial voids under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Interfacial voids and phase-separated regions degrade the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites during service.
A 50–100 nm Ni or Ni–Cu coating can be deposited on tungsten surfaces by magnetron sputtering before consolidation.
The coated W–Cu composite is to be consolidated by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1000°C under a controlled atmosphere.
The Ni-rich coating will induce formation of a graded Ni–W–Cu intermetallic interphase at the original W–Cu interface during sintering.
During sintering, the Ni-rich layer reacts with both tungsten and copper.
The graded Ni–W–Cu interphase acts as an effective diffusion barrier.
Excessive interdiffusion at the W–Cu interface causes phase separation.
Excessive interdiffusion at the W–Cu interface causes interfacial void formation.
A coating-induced graded interphase enhances interfacial bonding.
The graded Ni–W–Cu interphase will remain stable under thermal cycling.
The graded Ni–W–Cu interphase will remain stable under irradiation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have lower interfacial void density than untreated W–Cu composites.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation than untreated W–Cu composites.
The coating-induced microstructural changes will lower interfacial thermal resistance.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated composites after thermal cycling and irradiation.
The proposed treatment is applicable to service environments representative of joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
Variations in coating uniformity and interdiffusion kinetics could influence the resulting interphase and composite performance.
